journeys.name: Arctic to the Baltic
journeys.summary: Start where the sun does not set and end where medieval merchants counted their money. This is the long north: an Arctic city, an island chain of granite peaks, a night train down the spine of Sweden, and then the three old trading capitals of the Baltic — each of which was rich, then occupied, and is now itself again. Long legs, and the train is the point rather than the cost.

legs.why: Above the Arctic Circle: whales in winter, no darkness at all in June, and the best base in the north.
Peaks straight out of the sea and cod on racks. The one stop nobody regrets lengthening.
Over the border into Sweden's rain shadow, for the clearest skies in Lapland and the top of the Kungsleden.
The night train south delivers you to a capital on fourteen islands. Take the archipelago ferry.
Overnight boat across the gulf. Granite, design, and a public sauna on the water.
Two hours south by fast ferry into an intact medieval town wall.
The last leg by bus, into the largest Art Nouveau quarter in Europe.

pack: Waterproof shell and a warm layer for June — the Arctic does not read the calendar
Boots that will do a fell path as well as a city
An eye mask: it does not get dark
A card, not cash — the whole north is cashless
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: Atlantic to the Mediterranean
journeys.strapline: Across Iberia and along the coast
journeys.summary: The classic west-to-east traverse, taken slowly enough to notice the change: Atlantic light and salt cod in the northwest, the Moorish south in the middle, then the Mediterranean proper from Barcelona onward. Every leg on this route can be done by train, which is unusual for a journey of this length and is half the pleasure of it.

legs.why: Granite, port lodges and the Douro. Begin on the Atlantic, facing the wrong way on purpose.
Down the coast to tile, fado and the Gulbenkian. Three days is the minimum here.
Inland into the Alentejo: a Roman temple, a chapel of bones, and cork oaks in every direction.
Across the border into Andalusia. Orange trees, the Alcázar, and flamenco in a room of thirty.
East to the Alhambra, with the Sierra Nevada behind it and free tapas beneath it.
The long leg north by high-speed rail, into Gaudí's grid and the Mediterranean.
Over the border along the coast, for the light the painters came for.
The last hop east. Three thousand years, stacked, and the best street food of the trip.

pack: Comfortable shoes for cobbles and hills
Sun protection from April onwards
Something with sleeves for churches
A rail pass, or advance singles booked the day they open
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Alpine Grand Tour
journeys.strapline: Six valleys, four countries, one mountain range
journeys.summary: The Alps are a single range and five nationalities, and the way to feel that is to cross them slowly by train and cable car rather than fly over. This route runs west to east from Mont Blanc to the Dolomites, staying high, and every leg is on a scheduled public service. Book the mountain huts before you book the hotels.

legs.why: Under the highest mountain in western Europe, where alpinism was invented.
Car-free, under the Matterhorn, and reached by a rack railway from the valley.
Seventy-two waterfalls, cliff-shelf villages, and the Eiger across the valley.
East over the passes to the Engadin: sgraffito villages and 322 days of sun.
The Bernina and the Arlberg deliver you to a city with a 2,300-metre mountain at the tram stop.
South into the Dolomites and Ladin-speaking valleys, for the pink light on limestone at dawn.

pack: Boots with ankle support and a broken-in sole
Layers, and a hat, even in August
Cash for mountain huts, which often take nothing else
Sun cream — snow at altitude burns
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: Scandinavia to Central Europe
journeys.strapline: Copenhagen to Budapest, all by rail
journeys.summary: A north-south line down the middle of the continent, from a harbour you can swim in to a capital built on hot springs. It crosses the old inner-German border, the old iron curtain, and three empires' worth of architecture, without ever needing a flight or a car. The stretch from Berlin to Budapest is the densest run of great cities in Europe.

legs.why: Design, harbour swimming and smørrebrød. The northern end of the line.
Across the bridges into Germany's port city, and the Elbphilharmonie's free plaza.
Three hours south. The twentieth century, in the city that carried most of it.
Baroque rebuilt from rubble, on a river bend, with sandstone towers upstream.
Over the mountains into Bohemia: gothic, baroque, cubist, and the beer that explains the rest.
South to the imperial capital. Standing tickets at the opera, coffee house afternoons.
The last leg down the Danube, ending in a thermal bath in the snow if you time it right.

pack: An umbrella you do not mind losing
Comfortable shoes; these are walking cities
One smart layer for an opera house or a concert hall
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Adriatic Run
journeys.strapline: Venice to Dubrovnik the long way round
journeys.summary: Down the eastern Adriatic, which has the Mediterranean's clearest water and its least developed coastline. The route leaves the sea twice on purpose — into Slovenia's karst and into Bosnia — because the interior is where the layers are: Venetian, Ottoman, Habsburg and Yugoslav, sometimes in the same street. Ferries and buses, not trains, from Split onward.

legs.why: Begin on the wrong side of the sea, in the city that ruled the rest of this coast.
Inland to a small green capital, and the caves an hour beyond it.
Slovenia's 46 kilometres of coast, and a Venetian town on a spit with salt pans beside it.
Into Istria: truffles, olive oil and a campanile copied from San Marco.
South to a Roman emperor's palace that people still live inside.
Inland into Herzegovina, for a bridge that was destroyed and rebuilt from its own river.
Back to the water, at the head of a drowned canyon, with 1,350 steps up the wall behind it.
The last two hours north up the coast, into the walls. Walk them at opening.

pack: Water shoes — most of this coast is pebble or rock
A dry bag for boat legs
Shoulders and knees covered for churches and mosques
Sea-sickness tablets for the open crossings
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: Camino & Sacred Europe
journeys.strapline: Six places people have walked to for a thousand years
journeys.summary: Not a religious journey unless you want it to be — a route through the buildings and landscapes that pilgrimage produced, which is most of what Europe built before it built anything else. It ends where it should, on foot, in the rain, in Galicia. Two of these stops are still working monastic communities and one is a sovereign state.

legs.why: The English end: a cathedral, a murder in it, and a pilgrims' road out of London.
Across the Channel to 172 windows of twelfth-century glass and a labyrinth in the floor.
South to the city everything else was measured against, and the necropolis under the basilica.
East to six working monasteries on top of sandstone pillars, linked by monks' footpaths.
The long jump west, and the last hundred kilometres walked in from Sarria.

pack: Boots already broken in — this is not the trip to test them
A credencial if you intend to walk the last stage
Blister tape, before you need it
Something to cover shoulders in every church
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Hanseatic Arc
journeys.strapline: The medieval trading league, in order
journeys.summary: Between the 13th and 17th centuries a network of merchant towns ran the northern seas, and they all built with the same brick and the same confidence. This route follows them from Flanders to the Gulf of Finland. What the League left behind is a very specific pleasure: gabled warehouses, town halls larger than the towns needed, and a shared idea of what a rich city should look like.

legs.why: The southern end: a city that got rich, silted up, and was preserved by the accident.
North to the canal ring that came after the League and outdid it.
East to the queen of the Hanse herself, on an island, in brick gothic.
Along the Baltic to the Polish end of the network — and to 1939 and 1980.
Across the sea to the largest Art Nouveau quarter in Europe, built on the same trade.
The last stop: the wall, the towers and the guild halls, all still standing.

pack: A windproof layer; the Baltic is not warm even in July
Comfortable shoes for brick and cobble
A book for the ferry legs
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Classical Mediterranean
journeys.strapline: Greek and Roman cities, on both shores
journeys.summary: Three thousand years of the same sea. This route takes in the best-preserved classical cities on either side of the Mediterranean — a Sicilian cathedral built inside a Doric temple, a Roman arena still hosting events, and the Anatolian coast where more of the Greek world survives than in Greece. Two flights or ferries are unavoidable and are worth it.

legs.why: The obvious beginning, and still the right one.
South for the archaeological museum, which holds everything good from Pompeii, and the pizza.
Across to Sicily: Norman, Arab and Byzantine in one chapel ceiling.
Down the coast to the most powerful Greek city in the world, and a temple inside a cathedral.
East across the sea, for the Acropolis at opening and the museum afterwards.
On to Anatolia and Ephesus, where the library facade and the marble street still stand.

pack: A hat and real sun protection — the sites have no shade
Two litres of water capacity per person
Boots for Ephesus and the Sicilian sites
Modest dress for churches and mosques
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The European Heritage Route
journeys.summary: The specification's own suggestion, and a good one: the cathedral-and-capital spine of western and central Europe, taken entirely by train. It crosses seven countries and four architectural centuries without ever needing a flight, and every stop on it is a city that once thought of itself as the centre of something.
pack: A rail pass, or advance singles
One smart layer for a concert
An umbrella
Shoulders covered for churches

legs.why: Begin with the free national collections and a play for the price of a cinema ticket.
An hour out, and the mother church of a global communion.
Under the Channel and into Flanders: a city preserved by going broke in 1500.
The canal ring, the Rijksmuseum, and a bicycle rather than a tram.
Up the Rhine: a cathedral that took 632 years and a Roman city under the streets.
East into Bohemia, and the largest intact gothic and baroque centre north of the Alps.
South to the imperial capital: standing tickets at the opera, coffee houses in the afternoon.
Down the Danube to end in a thermal bath, ideally in the snow.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Mediterranean Arc
journeys.strapline: Barcelona to Athens along one sea
journeys.summary: Also from the specification: the northern shore of the Mediterranean, followed east. It changes language five times and cuisine about fifteen, and the through-line is a sea that everyone on it has been trading across for three thousand years. Ferries and trains for most of it; one flight at the end unless you have a spare week.
pack: Water shoes
Sun protection from May
A dry bag
Modest dress for churches

legs.why: Start where the Mediterranean meets a grid designed in 1859.
Over the border along the coast, into the light the painters came for.
Into Liguria and the five villages on the cliff coast.
Inland briefly, because it would be absurd not to.
South for the archaeological museum and the pizza that justifies the detour.
Across to Sicily: the most powerful Greek city in the world, once.
East across the Ionian, into Venetian Greece.
The end of the arc, and the beginning of most of what is on it.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Baltic Crossing
journeys.summary: A short, dense route round the eastern Baltic: three capitals that were occupied within living memory and one that was not, joined by ferries that locals use as buses. It is the cheapest good rail-and-boat trip in northern Europe and the least travelled by visitors from outside it.
pack: A windproof layer
Comfortable shoes for cobbles
A card — the region is nearly cashless

legs.why: Granite, design, and a public sauna on the water.
Two hours south by fast ferry into an intact medieval wall.
The largest Art Nouveau quarter in Europe, and a market in five Zeppelin hangars.
South again: forty churches, endless courtyards, and a republic of artists.
An island castle in a lake, an hour out, to finish on.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Danube Line
journeys.summary: The Danube passes through more capitals than any river in the world, and this follows the interesting half of it. Cycle path, train and river boat all run alongside each other for most of the way, so the transport is a choice rather than a constraint.
pack: A bicycle, if you want one — the path is flat the whole way
Sun protection on the water
One smart layer for Vienna

legs.why: Start in the Wachau: terraced vineyards and a blue baroque tower over the water.
Downstream to the imperial capital.
An hour further, and a different country with a castle on the bluff.
The river's best city, and its widest.
Into Serbia: a Habsburg river town under a fortress with sixteen kilometres of tunnels.
End where the Sava joins it, on a fortress above both.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Iberian Circle
journeys.strapline: Two countries, one peninsula, no flights
journeys.summary: A loop rather than a line: down the Atlantic, across the Moorish south, up the Mediterranean and back through the middle. High-speed rail makes the long legs painless and the slow legs are where the trip actually is.
pack: Comfortable shoes
Sun protection and a hat from May
A siesta-shaped attitude to the afternoon

legs.why: Begin on the Atlantic, with port lodges across the river.
Down the coast: tiles, fado and the Gulbenkian.
Inland into the Alentejo, and a Roman temple in a walled town.
Across the border into Andalusia.
East, to the Alhambra and free tapas.
North up the Mediterranean for paella where the rice grows.
The last coastal stop, and the densest three days of the route.
Inland to finish: the Prado, vermouth at noon, and a train home.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Carpathian Arc
journeys.strapline: Mountains, monasteries and very few visitors
journeys.summary: The Carpathians run 1,500 kilometres through five countries and almost nobody outside them treats the range as one thing. This does. Wooden churches, painted monasteries, hay meadows cut by hand, brown bears, and prices that make western Europe look absurd.
pack: Boots
A torch for unlit churches
Cash for village guesthouses
Layers — the range makes its own weather

legs.why: Start in the city, then go east and stop seeing anyone.
Into the Tatras, Poland's only alpine range.
Over the border into Slovakia and the same mountains under another name.
Down into the Spiš: a walled town under the largest castle ruin in central Europe.
South into Transylvania and the Saxon citadels.
A single-street village with a fortified church and horses on the road.
Under a wooded mountain, with a bear hide bookable at dusk.
North into Bucovina, to painted monasteries that have kept their colour for five centuries.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The Cold North
journeys.strapline: Winter, treated as the reason rather than the problem
journeys.summary: Most of Europe's north is sold in summer and is more itself in February. This is a winter route: aurora, snow, saunas, ice and four hours of daylight that are better than most places get in twelve. It needs proper clothing and repays it.
pack: Proper insulated boots, not fashion boots
Mittens, not gloves
A merino base layer
Something to cover your face at −25°C
Patience: the aurora is a forecast, not a booking

legs.why: Start with a sauna on the frozen waterfront.
North by night train, into Lapland proper.
Sámi Finland, a lake with three thousand islands, and no light pollution in any direction.
Across into Norway for whales in the dark and the aurora directly overhead.
South-east into the driest winter sky in Lapland, and the chairlift into it.
End in the iron town that is being physically moved off the hole it dug.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: The White South
journeys.strapline: Andalusia and the Maghreb's long shadow
journeys.summary: Eight centuries of Islamic rule left more than the Alhambra, and this route is the rest of it: the horseshoe arch in the village church, the irrigation channel still running, the word for the vegetable. Short legs, hot afternoons, and everything happening after six.
pack: A hat
A siesta
Shoes for cobbled hills
Modest dress for the mosque-cathedral

legs.why: Start with the Alcázar and a flamenco peña.
An hour and a half north-east, for 856 columns.
East to the last Moorish city in Spain.
West into the white villages, over a 120-metre gorge.
To the Atlantic, and possibly the oldest city in western Europe.
Back east along the coast, to finish with Picasso and grilled sardines.

journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial

journeys.name: Arctic to Mediterranean
journeys.strapline: The full length of Europe, 69°N to 38°N
journeys.summary: The specification's flagship, and the longest thing on this site: the whole north-to-south axis of Europe, from the midnight sun to the Aegean. Thirteen stops, eight countries, and roughly 5,000 kilometres of ground. Almost all of it can be done by train, which is the argument for taking it slowly rather than flying the middle out. It is a month, and it is honestly a month — anyone selling you this in a fortnight is selling you airports.
journeys.creator: EuropeDoor editorial
pack: Layers for both ends: it is 8°C in Tromsø and 32°C in Athens on the same trip
A rail pass, and the patience to reserve the legs that need reserving
Boots that will do a fell in Norway and a marble street in Rome
An eye mask for the north and a hat for the south

legs.why: Begin at 69°N, where the sun does not set in June and does not rise in December.
South-west into the islands: granite straight out of the sea, cod on racks.
Over the border into Sweden by the Iron Ore Line, through Lapland.
The night train south, to a capital on fourteen islands.
Across the Öresund bridge into Denmark.
Into Germany, and Europe's third port.
East to the city that carried most of the twentieth century.
South to the imperial capital, and the first hint of the south.
Over the Alps into the Dolomites, and Ladin-speaking valleys.
Down out of the mountains to the lagoon.
South through Italy to the city everything else was measured against.
Further south, for the archaeological museum and the pizza.
Across the sea to the end of the line.
